description:
We are a team of curious students passionate about space exploration, technology, and storytelling. Through Cosmic Archive, we aim to create an interactive digital experience that brings attention to forgotten spacecraft, landers, rovers, and other human-made objects left beyond Earth. Our goal is to make space history engaging and accessible through research, web development, interactive visuals, and creative storytelling.

Languages: English, Urdu
summary: Space Time Capsule is a friendly, visual website that tells the stories of human-made machines left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space. Built for school-age students, it turns NASA's discarded hardware into "space time capsules" — each one frozen in time, holding the story of the day humans left it there. Visitors explore an interactive map with world-switcher tabs, a glowing timeline, and a searchable collection of 14 missions, including Apollo 11, Viking 1 and 2, Phoenix, InSight, Perseverance, Ingenuity, Pioneer 10, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, and Kepler. Every fact comes only from NASA, checked against the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive and the challenge's 14 official resources, with real NASA photos and their photo IDs. It addresses the challenge by making forgotten hardware memorable, simple, and fun to explore — so a child can tap a glowing dot, read a story, and understand why that machine still matters.
details: Space Time Capsule is a 5-page front-end website (Home, Interactive Map, Mission Timeline, Hardware Collection, Sources & Learning) with no backend, accounts, or API keys. It works on phone, tablet, and desktop, with large touch targets, keyboard access, and reduced-motion support. Each mission story explains in simple words what the machine did, why it is important, its impact, and what we learned from it. It was built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using local data and real NASA photos from NASA's Image and Video Library. It is creative because it frames abandoned hardware as time capsules and uses the punchline "Abandoned — but never forgotten." The team considered accuracy first (NASA-only facts), simplicity for young readers, and accessibility for all devices.
